name: Friedrich Hayek
role: Austrian-British economist and political philosopher, Nobel laureate in economics (1974)
summary: Hayek argues that knowledge is dispersed, so competition and prices coordinate economic life better than central planning, and that collectivism of every kind leads toward totalitarian control. He wants government bound by general rules, a safety net and public goods but no "social justice" redistribution, a market order with competing private currencies, and a constitution that separates rule-making from administration. He prefers limited democracy but ranked liberal institutions above democratic form, as his 1981 Chile remarks show.

notes: Read in full or in large part: The Road to Serfdom, The Fatal Conceit, "Why I Am Not a Conservative", "The Use of Knowledge in Society", Denationalisation of Money (Argument Refined). The Constitution of Liberty and Law, Legislation and Liberty could not be opened as primary texts, so what they say is taken from scholarly guides (Miller, IEA/Butler, Hamowy) and rated medium at most. Hayek held no office and has no votes or speeches in the record corpora, so every answer rests on his words, plus the Chile visits as reported by Caldwell and Montes. Searched themes: economy (planning, money, trade, taxes, welfare, unions, housing, farming), government (democracy, rule of law, constitution, emergencies), social (conservatism, religion, change). Immigration, abortion, drugs, guns, family, gender, race, environment and most foreign-policy and religion statements had no recorded position in these sources. The Constitution of Liberty and Law, Legislation and Liberty themselves, and his other essays, were not searched directly.
